findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is in plain words. That is all the page says about Athena itself. Who it is for, what it needs to run (models, keys, platforms), and why to pick it over other tools are never said.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This is the Athena site, but nearly all of the page is a deep study of a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to work out from the third lede paragraph that the page is a demonstration, not Athena's documentation.

The page does say why it matters and then delivers on it. Every statement carries claim ids, and each claim links to exact file lines at a pinned commit, so a reader can check the selling point for themselves.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The next step is easy to find: the header links to it and a section at the end lists it. But the install instructions leave out how to get the checkout and what to have installed first. A newcomer has to go to the GitHub repository to actually start.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself."; Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: The 'Start here' section is the most readable part for a newcomer. It defines the key terms before using them, gives a one-sentence summary of firstmate, and walks through one numbered task from start to finish.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: Several terms are used without being defined, even though the glossary is long: endpoint, durable record, heartbeat (claim c9), crewmate (c44), and harness pin. A newcomer stalls on these in the transition cards.
findings.source: t8 card: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead"; t1 summary: "the prior durable record is restored" (from 'When things go wrong')

findings.text: The state, counter and transition sections are written for someone reasoning about firstmate's internals, such as exit codes and lock behaviour. They are thorough but far too detailed for a first visit, and nothing says a newcomer can skip them.
findings.source: Transitions: "the spawn script finds every capacity place held (decided by code)" ... "capacity full (exit 75)"

findings.text: The page is open about what it does not know: it flags gaps in the source and says the study read the code but never ran it. A newcomer trying to judge whether Athena can be trusted gets an honest picture.
findings.source: in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."; Limits of this study: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
